name: configuration
intro: Every environment variable XTM One reads at startup, on the platform and on the worker. Authentication, integrations and most security options are set from the **Settings** screens instead, and stored in the database.

cells: JWT signing + Fernet encryption key. Generate with `python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))"`. Never change after deployment.
Default admin account email. Created or updated on every startup: the account is also made an administrator and re-enabled each time, so it stays a way back into the platform.
Default admin account password. Reset to this value on every startup. At most 72 bytes (what bcrypt stores); a longer value is refused at startup.
Programmatic API token for the admin (must start with `fcp-`, min 32 chars). Like every bcrypt-hashed key, only its first 72 bytes are checked.

Proxy addresses allowed to set `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-For`, as an IP, CIDR or comma-separated list. Set this behind a TLS-terminating proxy: without it the platform sees every request as plain HTTP from the proxy's address, which records the proxy's address in the audit log for every user, makes the A2A endpoints refuse every request (`403 https required`), makes `/runners/enroll`, `/mcp/oauth/register` and `/mcp/oauth/token` log an unconfirmed-transport warning (they refuse too only under `CREDENTIAL_TRANSPORT_STRICT`), and collapses per-IP rate limiting into one shared bucket. Name the proxy as the platform container sees it (see Client address and protocol behind the proxy). Hostnames are not resolved and a CIDR needs its host bits at zero (`10.42.0.0/16`, not `10.42.0.1/16`): uvicorn keeps any other entry as a literal that matches no peer, and the platform names such entries in a startup warning. uvicorn reads it from the platform container's environment when the platform starts, so it is not a Settings > Access and security field and a change needs a restart; the shipped `docker-compose.yml` passes it to the platform container. When audited requests come through a peer it does not name, the platform logs a warning naming that peer and the security audit reports it (see Client addresses in the audit trail). Prefer it over `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS`; avoid `*`, which lets any caller choose its own `scope["client"]`; it means "every peer" only as the whole value.

When `true`, the platform takes the client address from the leftmost `X-Forwarded-For` value and the scheme from `X-Forwarded-Proto`, from any peer and ahead of `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`. Behind a proxy that appends to `X-Forwarded-For` that value is whatever the client sent, so a caller can choose its rate-limit bucket and the address the audit trail records: enable it only behind a proxy that overwrites the header and is the only thing that reaches the platform, and prefer `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`. While it is on the platform logs a warning at startup (or when it is switched on in Settings > Access and security) and the security audit warns that forwarded headers are trusted from any peer. Switching to `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`: [UPGRADING.md](https://github.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one/blob/main/UPGRADING.md) and Client address and protocol behind the proxy. The shipped `docker-compose.yml` does not pass the variable to the platform container. Also in **Settings > Access and security** (**Trust proxy headers**); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Prefix length the per-IP rate limits (login, forgot and reset password, invitation registration, MFA verification, A2A pre-authentication, MCP OAuth registration, authorization and token, the public chat widget, Content Security Policy violation reports) key a native IPv6 client on. `128` keeps one bucket per address. `64` is opt-in: it stops a client drawing a fresh bucket from every address of the /64 it is handed, but every device of one /64 - a corporate IPv6 LAN, for example - then shares one budget. From `32` to `128`; any other value stops the platform at startup. The key in use is logged once at startup, and the security audit reports an info finding recommending `64` while the value is above `64`. IPv4 clients (IPv4-mapped included) are always keyed per address, and the audit trail, the access log and the webhook diagnostics always record the full address. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Opt-in: key, log and store every client address (the `X-Forwarded-For` hop under `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS`, the peer otherwise) in its canonical form - port, brackets and IPv6 zone index dropped, an IPv4-mapped address read as IPv4, IPv6 lowercase and compressed - so one client is one rate-limit key whatever the proxy wrote; behind a proxy that writes `IP:port` under `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS`, every connection is otherwise its own bucket. `false` uses an address as it was read, as in earlier releases. Either way a value that is not an IP address is ignored, with a warning logged once, and an address longer than the audit trail's 45 characters is stored in canonical form. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Opt-in. By default `/runners/enroll`, `/mcp/oauth/register` and `/mcp/oauth/token` serve a request whose transport the platform cannot confirm encrypted, with the answers of earlier releases, and log it once per route (`... served over unconfirmed transport ...`). `true` refuses such a request the way the A2A endpoints do, before reading it or issuing anything: `/runners/enroll` answers `403 {"detail": "https required"}`, `/mcp/oauth/register` answers `400 {"error": "invalid_client_metadata", "error_description": "https required"}` (RFC 7591), `/mcp/oauth/token` answers `400 {"error": "invalid_request", "error_description": "https required"}`. Real loopback stays exempt under `DEBUG` or `A2A_ALLOW_INSECURE_LOOPBACK`, and so do the end-to-end suite's `TEST_ONLY_INSECURE_TRANSPORT_PEERS`. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, set `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` first and check the warning no longer appears. The security audit reports `network.credential_transport_strict_off` while it is off - a warning while the platform is served over plain HTTP (`BASE_URL` not https, `DEBUG` off) and an active runner or a registered MCP OAuth client holds credentials those routes issued, information otherwise - and `network.credential_transport_strict_on` (pass) when it is on. Also in **Settings > Access and security** (**Require HTTPS for runner enrollment and MCP tokens**); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

**Testing only.** Count a plain HTTP request from real loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`) as encrypted, so the A2A endpoints accept it: what lets a deployment federated with itself reach its own agent card without terminating TLS. Only the real socket peer counts: a request carrying `X-Forwarded-For` is never exempt. Never set it behind a reverse proxy on the same host, where every request arrives from loopback. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

**Local development only.** Comma-separated origins (`scheme://host[:port]`) that outbound A2A requests may reach over plain HTTP and at addresses the destination guard otherwise refuses (loopback, private networks), to exercise the outbound half against a second deployment on the same machine. Every other destination stays refused, a listed origin is still pinned, and cloud metadata addresses stay refused even when listed. A malformed entry stops the platform at startup, and a configured list is logged at `WARNING` on every boot (and when it is saved in Settings > Access and security). Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Opt-in strict checks on OAuth token URLs. Every OAuth token request (authorization-code exchange and token refresh, for integrations and MCP servers) checks its token URL, both when the URL is saved and before each request, and every address its host resolves to. By default only a cloud-metadata address (`169.254.169.254` and the other instance-metadata endpoints) and a URL no request can be sent to (no host, an unreadable URL, port or host, a scheme other than `http`, `https`, `ws` or `wss`) are refused, so every token URL that worked before keeps working, loopback included. Set to `true` to also refuse token URLs on loopback, link-local, unspecified, reserved and multicast addresses, and any scheme other than `http` or `https`; private networks stay allowed, so an on-prem identity provider keeps working. A refusal names the setting that lifts it. Before turning it on, point every token URL on loopback at another address of the identity provider (a private-network address or a Docker service name such as `http://keycloak:8080`), or list its origin in `OAUTH_TOKEN_DEV_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` on a development machine. **Upgrading:** no action required; the strict mode is opt-in. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

**Local development only.** With the strict checks on (`OAUTH_TOKEN_URL_STRICT`), comma-separated origins (`scheme://host[:port]`) whose OAuth token URL may resolve to a loopback address. Listing an origin lifts the loopback refusal for that origin only; link-local and metadata addresses stay refused. No effect while the strict checks are off, which accept loopback token URLs anyway. A malformed entry stops the platform at startup, and a configured list is logged at `WARNING` on every boot (and when it is saved in Settings > Access and security), or at `INFO` as having no effect when `OAUTH_TOKEN_URL_STRICT=false` is set. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Which addresses a remote MCP server (`sse`, `streamable_http`) may be reached at. Checked when its URL is saved (the form, the agent builder, every import: a `422`) and on the address every connection to it actually opens - the connectivity test, tool calls, the authorization probe and OAuth discovery and registration included - with no second DNS lookup, each redirect hop checked again. `permissive` refuses only cloud metadata addresses (`169.254.169.254` and the other instance-metadata endpoints), so every MCP server that worked before keeps working, one on `localhost` included. `private_networks` also refuses loopback, link-local, unspecified, reserved and multicast addresses; private networks stay allowed, so an on-prem MCP server keeps working. `public_only` refuses every address that is not globally routable: reach an on-prem server through a relay group instead, whose relay checks its own allow-list. A cloud metadata address is refused in every mode, and a URL must be `http` or `https` with a host. A refusal answers one generic message (the address and its class go to the backend log only). A server routed through a relay group is judged only on what its URL spells. Behind an outbound proxy (`HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` applied), `permissive` keeps sending through it after refusing a URL that is, or resolves from the platform to, a metadata address; the stricter modes never use the proxy and connect directly, since the address connected to is what they judge. A server already saved at a refused address stops connecting until its URL changes or its origin is listed in `MCP_SERVER_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`; saving it without changing its URL, transport or relay group still works. A blank value is unset (`docker-compose.yml` forwards it to the platform and the worker). **Upgrading:** no action required; the stricter modes are opt-in. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Under `MCP_SERVER_URL_POLICY=private_networks` or `public_only`, comma-separated origins (`scheme://host[:port]`) a remote MCP server may be reached at whatever address they resolve to - an internal MCP server you vouch for. Matched on the origin: `http://mcp.internal:8080` covers every path on that service and nothing on another port, scheme or host. Cloud metadata addresses stay refused for a listed origin. No effect under `permissive`, which accepts those addresses anyway. A malformed entry stops the platform at startup. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Content-Security-Policy on every HTML page the platform serves. `report-only` blocks nothing: browsers report what the policy would have blocked to `/api/v1/csp-report`, where the reports are counted and logged; the security audit lists the violations of the last 7 days. `enforce` sends the same policy as `Content-Security-Policy`, so browsers block what it does not allow. `off` sends no policy. Any other value fails startup. See Security headers.

Origins, besides the platform itself and the platforms registered with it (only when `PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN` is a value of your own, and at most 20 of them), allowed to show the platform's pages in an iframe once the policy is enforced (an intranet portal, for instance). Comma-separated CSP sources: `https://portal.example.com`, `https://*.example.com`. A malformed entry fails startup; one that admits every site (`*`, `https:`, `https://*`) is accepted but logged as a warning at startup. See Security headers.

Declares a secret vault named `<name>` (`hashicorp`, `aws`, `gcp`, `azure` or `onepassword`) in the environment, for a deployment managed as code. Vaults are otherwise connected and granted in Settings > Access and security > Secret vaults, with no variable and no restart. Its other settings are `SECRET_VAULT_<NAME>_<SETTING>` (`ADDRESS`, `AUTH_METHOD`, `TOKEN_FILE`, `REGION`, `WRITERS`, `PATHS`, ...). Read once at startup, on the platform and the worker; listed read-only in Settings. See Secret vaults.

How long a value read from a vault is kept in memory, per process, for a vault with no cache duration of its own: a secret rotated in the vault is used once this time has passed, or at once when an integration's service refuses the cached value. `0` reads the vault on every use. See Secret vaults.

Comma-separated origins (`scheme://host[:port]`) that a vault connected in Settings > Access and security > Secret vaults may reach on a loopback address: an on-host vault. Such a vault's address is otherwise refused on loopback, link-local, reserved and cloud metadata addresses, checked when it is saved, tested and on every connection; private networks are allowed. Link-local and metadata addresses stay refused for a listed origin. Environment only, never a Settings field. A malformed entry stops the platform at startup. See Secret vaults.

Public URL of the platform. Used for OAuth/SAML callbacks and email links, and as the issuer of the tokens XTM One signs for OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ - set the same value on the worker. Includes the path prefix when `BASE_PATH` is set (`https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one`). Left unset outside Docker Compose, it falls back to `http://localhost:8100`; unset or empty, it is warned about at startup unless `DEBUG=true`.
Public URL of the frontend. Usually same as `BASE_URL`.

Comma-separated URLs the connected platforms reach XTM One on when they differ from `BASE_URL` (`http://xtm-one:4000` in Docker Compose), accepted as the audience of their tokens. An entry that is not an http(s) URL, or that carries credentials, a query or a fragment, fails startup. See Public and internal URLs.

URL path prefix when a reverse proxy serves the platform somewhere other than the root of its host: `/xtm-one` for `https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one/`. Works whether the proxy forwards the prefix or strips it (an `X-Forwarded-Prefix` header naming the prefix marks a stripped request). `BASE_URL` and `FRONTEND_URL` must include the same prefix. A plain path of ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, `~` (no percent-encoding); a prefix colliding with a namespace the platform serves itself (`/api`, `/v1`, `/mcp`, `/xtm`, `/a2a`, `/office`, `/metrics`, `/assets`, `/.well-known`) or with the name of one of its static files (`/favicon.ico`, `/logos`, `/robots.txt`, ...) is refused at startup; one that is also the address of a platform page (`/tools`, `/agents`, ...) is refused unless `BASE_PATH_MODE` declares the proxy. See Serving under a path prefix.

What the reverse proxy does with `BASE_PATH`. `auto` infers the shape of every request (the `X-Forwarded-Prefix` header, then the path) and refuses a `BASE_PATH` that is also a platform page, which the inference cannot resolve behind a stripping proxy. `forwarded` declares that the proxy keeps the prefix; `stripped` declares that it removes it and sends `X-Forwarded-Prefix` (Traefik's `StripPrefix` does, nginx needs `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix /xtm-one;`). Either declaration lifts the refusal.
`xtm_one` is the open standalone platform. Set `ai_disabled` to start with AI switched off — see Running without AI.

Shared secret OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ present (`Authorization: Bearer`) to register with XTM One - registration is also their heartbeat - and to unregister. Must match across services. Generate one with `python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"`. Unset, every registration is refused. `docker-compose.yml` falls back to the published value `xtm-default-registration-token`, accepted only so the platforms already registered stay connected - it cannot register a new platform, change a registered platform's URL, rename one, change what one declares or unregister one - and logged as a warning at startup and reported as a critical finding by the security audit (`Settings` → `Security`) until you set your own; meanwhile the Filigran license certificate is withheld from registration answers. After 10 failed attempts in a minute, a client is refused (HTTP 429) until the minute ends. See Upgrade and XTM Suite integration.

Enterprise license PEM. Can also be configured from Settings UI. Set it on the platform and on the worker: a worker without it runs its background AI on the licensed verdict the platform publishes, and logs a warning once.

How long background AI work that comes due while AI is unavailable (Community Edition, or AI switched off) is held before it is failed with the reason. Held work (a delayed or queued assignment run, a run resumed from a human-review pause, a background task that had not started, the pending runs of an evaluation) is shown as **Held**, is never charged, and runs by itself within about five minutes of AI being available again. The same bound applies to a due assignment run or background task held while the quota store cannot be reached and quotas fail closed. `0` fails such work at its start instead of holding it.
Display name override. DB value takes precedence.
Logo override (data URI). DB value takes precedence.
Full asyncpg connection string. Override when using external PostgreSQL.
Password for the bundled PostgreSQL container.
Extra connections allowed beyond pool size.
Seconds a request waits for a free pooled connection.
Seconds after which a pooled connection is replaced, so connections a firewall or proxy dropped silently are not reused.
Seconds allowed to open one connection.

How long a new connection keeps being retried while PostgreSQL refuses or drops it (restart, failover, a Service briefly without a ready endpoint). Requests and LLM trace writes wait instead of failing; past it requests get a `503` with `Retry-After` instead of a `500`. A timed-out connect is never retried. `0` disables.

Longest wait for a lock by a statement of the database migrations at startup. Past it the migration is retried, then startup fails with an error instead of waiting forever. It replaces a `lock_timeout` set on the database role or the database (`ALTER ROLE ... SET`) for the migration connection, a tighter one included; `0` keeps that one, or no limit when none is set.

Longest run of a statement of the database migrations at startup. Past it the migration is retried once, then startup fails with an error naming this setting. Raise it if an upgrade of a very large database fails on a statement timeout. Like the lock timeout, it replaces a `statement_timeout` set on the role or the database; `0` keeps that one.

When the platform has not completed its startup after this many seconds, it logs an error naming the step in progress and the database sessions blocking the migration, then repeats it at the same interval. After the same delay, the worker's wait for the database migration turns into an error when no platform process is migrating the database. `0` disables.
Redis connection string. Override for external Redis.
Password of the Sentinel nodes, separate from the Redis password.
Redis ACL user. In standalone mode it can also be part of `REDIS_URL`.

The number of the Redis database to use, in sentinel mode only (in standalone mode, put it at the end of `REDIS_URL`, as in `redis://redis:6379/2`). `0`, the default, keeps the Redis default database.
TLS to Redis in Sentinel mode. In standalone mode use a `rediss://` URL instead.
The path, inside the container, of the CA bundle that verifies the certificates of Redis and its Sentinels when `REDIS_SSL` is `true`. Unset, the system's certificate authorities are used.
Connections in the shared pool of each process.

The memory cap of the Redis container that the product's own `docker-compose.yml` starts, such as `512mb` (`256mb` when unset). Past it, Redis evicts the least recently used keys. The platform does not read it; size a Redis you run yourself in its own configuration.
Whether the certificate of the S3 endpoint is verified when `S3_USE_SSL` is `true` (on by default). Set it to `false` only for an endpoint with a self-signed certificate.

Take AWS credentials from the pod or instance role (EKS IRSA or Pod Identity, ECS task role, EC2 instance profile) instead of `S3_ACCESS_KEY` / `S3_SECRET_KEY`, which are then ignored. The role needs `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` on the bucket objects, `s3:ListBucket` for the bucket check, `s3:GetBucketLocation` when `S3_REGION` is empty, and `s3:CreateBucket` if the platform creates the bucket. Presigned URLs carry the role session token, so they expire with that session (1 hour by default on EKS) even when `S3_PRESIGNED_EXPIRY` is longer.

API key for the named provider. Re-applied on every startup (env wins). The provider shows an **Env** badge in **Settings → AI Models**; removing the variable and restarting is what removes it (deleting it from the UI, where that is allowed, only lasts until the next restart).

Comma-separated list of models to expose. Either pinned or an editable baseline, depending on `LLM_PROVIDER_MODELS_EDITABLE`. When unset, the provider's stored model list is never touched by the startup seed. A provider that lists no model chats on its built-in chat model only while no configured provider lists one: next to providers whose models are listed, it takes no chat and no failover. A key set for the image, video, speech or music models alone (`DEFAULT_*_PROVIDER` below) therefore needs no model list.

`false`: the `*_MODELS` list **is** the catalog — it overwrites the provider's models on every startup, the **Models** editor is hidden for env-seeded providers and the API refuses model changes on them (403). `true`: the `*_MODELS` list is a **baseline** — seeded on first startup, then only its changes are applied on later restarts (models added to the variable are added, models removed from it are removed, every other edit made in **Settings → AI Models** is kept), and administrators can curate the models of env-seeded providers from the UI. The API key stays env-managed and the provider still cannot be deleted from the UI.

When `true`, all LLM provider management from the UI/API is disabled (add, edit, rename, delete return 403); providers are defined only through `LLM_PROVIDER_*` variables. Overrides `LLM_PROVIDER_MODELS_EDITABLE`, and is itself overridden by `BYOLLM_ACTIVATED`.

**Bring your own LLM** — the administrator owns the LLM configuration. When `true`: administrators add and manage providers and their keys from **Settings → AI Models** (implies `LLM_PROVIDER_MODELS_EDITABLE=true`, overrides `MODELS_ENV_PROVIDING_ONLY=true` with a startup warning naming both), and every `DEFAULT_*` value **furnishes an install once** — applied at startup only to an install that has no LLM configuration of its own yet, and inert from the first thing an administrator stores, so no restart can take a choice back (including the choice to leave a field empty). The matching controls stay editable with no **Env** badge, embedding and image defaults included. Provider API keys stay environment-managed either way.

Platform-wide default model. Re-applied on every startup when a configured provider still offers it (a warning is logged otherwise and the current default is kept). Under `BYOLLM_ACTIVATED=true` it only furnishes an install that has no LLM configuration yet.

Provider type images are generated with (`openai`, `gemini`, `elevenlabs`, `custom_openai`, `litellm`). Re-applied on every startup with `DEFAULT_IMAGE_MODEL`, and **Settings → AI Models → Image Generation** shows an **Env** badge.
Image model (for example `gpt-image-2`). Set alone, only the model is re-applied, on whichever provider serves it.
Base URL of a `custom_openai` or `litellm` image endpoint, composed with that provider's API key.

Provider type that reads answers aloud in the chat and narrates Video Studio videos (`openai`, `gemini`, `elevenlabs`, `azure_openai`, `litellm`, ...). Same rules as `DEFAULT_VIDEO_PROVIDER`; locks **Settings → AI Models → Speech Generation**, voice included. When unset, a voice generator such as ElevenLabs speaks first, else the first provider with a built-in speech model.
Speech model of `DEFAULT_SPEECH_PROVIDER` (for example `tts-1-hd` or `gpt-4o-mini-tts` on `openai`).
Voice id or name of `DEFAULT_SPEECH_PROVIDER` (an ElevenLabs voice id, `alloy` on OpenAI, ...). People can still choose their own voice where the chat offers it.

Provider type the Video Studio composes AI music with (`gemini`, `elevenlabs`, `filigran_gateway`). Same rules as `DEFAULT_VIDEO_PROVIDER`; locks **Settings → AI Models → Music Generation**. When unset, the first provider with a built-in music model composes.
Music model of `DEFAULT_MUSIC_PROVIDER` (for example `lyria-3.5` on `gemini`; name it on `filigran_gateway`, which has no built-in model).

Provider type serving the decision model agents use to act on the host page of an embedded chat (`openai`, `openrouter`, `ollama`, `filigran_gateway`, `custom_openai`, and `lmstudio` once an LM Studio integration feeds it). Requires `DEFAULT_DECISION_MODEL`; locks **Settings → AI Models → Decision Model**. Without `DEFAULT_DECISION_MODEL`, or with another provider type, it is logged at startup and ignored, and the section stays editable. When unset, agents cannot act on the host page until an administrator picks a decision model.
Decision model of `DEFAULT_DECISION_PROVIDER`. Decision models are seldom listed by their provider, so the id is used as written.

Hands the thinking blocks of the current tool round back to the Anthropic models that think by default (Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5, Mythos), so a tool round resumes with the reasoning that asked for the tools. A turn's blocks are re-sent unmodified only while the system prompt, the tools and the earlier messages are exactly those they were produced under; any change (a tool group loaded mid-run, an older tool result cleared, a compaction) sends the turn without them, as when the setting is off. A request the API refuses over them is sent again without them, so the setting never fails a turn. Every LLM generation whose request carries earlier thinking records what was re-sent and why not in its `thinking_replay` trace metadata, with the setting off too - compare a period with the setting on against one with it off before enabling it for good.
`The first configured of OpenAI, Gemini, Azure OpenAI, Mistral, Bedrock and Ollama`
Provider type knowledge bases and memory are embedded with. Re-applied on every startup with `DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_MODEL`, and **Settings → AI Models → Embedding** becomes read-only.

The embedding model the platform uses, instead of the one detected from the configured provider, usually with `DEFAULT_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`. It is applied again on every startup, and the embedding control of Settings > AI and models > Models becomes read-only.
Base URL of a `custom_openai`, `litellm` or `tei` embedding endpoint, composed with that provider's API key.
Smaller vector size, for models that support it (for example `1536` instead of `3072`).
Model that decides mandatory handovers between agents. Locks its control in **Settings → AI Models**.
Model tried first when the main model keeps failing (rate limit, overload). Locks its control in **Settings → AI Models**.
Default reasoning effort of reasoning models: `low`, `medium`, `high` or `max`. Locks its control in **Settings → AI Models**.
Chat model of the General Assistant. Locks its control in **Settings → General Assistant**.
Anthropic prompt caching: the repeated start of each request (tools, instructions, earlier messages) is billed at the cache rate.
How long a cached prefix lives: `5m` or `1h` (twice the write cost, worth it for conversations with long pauses, such as approvals or channels).
Uvicorn worker processes. Production: `2 × CPU cores + 1`.

Requests a web worker receives before it is replaced (`0` = never), plus up to `MAX_REQUESTS_JITTER` (default half of it). A worker past its quota keeps serving until no agent turn runs in it, so a recycle never cuts a chat turn; the pod stays up and the replacement starts at once. The replacement skips the migrations and the seeding already applied since the container started, and holds the requests it receives while it starts (see Health probes).

How long a worker past its `MAX_REQUESTS` quota waits for the agent turns running in it (chat turns, wakes after background work, channel messages) before it recycles anyway. `0` recycles at the quota, cutting the turns still running after `GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT`.

Seconds a stopping web worker (a recycle, a deployment, a scale-in) gives the requests and agent turns it runs to finish. A chat turn still running then is cut: it stores a reply naming what stopped it and the tool calls it had completed, and the conversation offers to resume it.
Concurrent queued jobs (document processing and indexing) per worker container. Agent runs are bounded separately by `MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS` and `MAX_CONCURRENT_SUB_AGENT_TASKS`.
Longest run, in seconds, of a queued worker job. Document processing has its own, longer bound.

Seconds a stopping worker gives its in-flight jobs to finish. Keep it about 10 seconds below the container's kill deadline (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in Kubernetes, `stop_grace_period` in Docker Compose, both 30 seconds by default). `0` cancels them at once.
Requests one platform process handles at once. Above it, requests get a fast `429` instead of queuing; health probes are exempt. `0` disables it.

Incoming channel messages (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Google Chat) one platform process answers at once; the others wait their turn. Keep it well below `DB_POOL_SIZE` + `DB_MAX_OVERFLOW`.
A run still active after this long logs a warning. `0` disables the warning.
A run nobody is working on any more (its worker or platform process stopped) is failed after this long, and what it held is released.

The lease a background task (a sub-agent delegation) runs under, renewed every third of it. At least three times the longest tool call of an agent turn, so a single long call (a wait, a CI poll, a large read) never costs the task its attempt; a worker that died is recovered after that long. `0` uses `ORCHESTRATION_LEASE_SECONDS`.
Dedicated slots for autonomous attack-path runs, separate from the assignment/sub-agent pool so dozens can run in parallel without starving normal execution. `0` shares the pool.
Max decision cycles an autonomous run chains back-to-back before briefly yielding, so a multi-step engagement doesn't stall between cycles.
Wall-clock budget for that back-to-back burst (whichever limit is reached first triggers the yield).

How often a run waiting on operator input re-checks for an answer or stop. Each unanswered re-check doubles the next interval, up to `AUTONOMOUS_WAITING_INPUT_RECHECK_MAX_SECONDS`. `0` waits purely for the operator's reply.
Longest interval between two re-checks of a run waiting on operator input. An operator answer still resumes the run at once.

How often the worker re-checks whether an in-flight run was stopped, so an operator Stop aborts the running agent within seconds instead of after the current decision cycle finishes. `0` falls back to the slower lease-heartbeat detection.

The worker pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (Docker Compose: its `stop_grace_period`), as its deployment sets it. With `WORKER_STARTUP_SECONDS`, how long a render the worker hands back when it is stopped waits for the next worker: first in the queue, it is failed only once neither its old worker nor a new one could have taken it. It also bounds how long a stopping worker waits for its renders to finish (`VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_DRAIN_SECONDS`). `0` = not given: 30 s, the Kubernetes default. Never less than 3 minutes together. `docker-compose.yml` sets `1260` for its workers.

How long a new worker pod may take to start: its startup probe's `initialDelaySeconds` plus `failureThreshold` x `periodSeconds`, with the image pull if it is slow. `0` = not given: 570 s, so a deployment that sets neither lets a render wait 10 minutes. A render that waited longer fails naming the workers alive and why none took it; rendering it again at the same quality within a day resumes the same render from the frames it kept.

Days the pictures an assistant makes to check its own work (frames and region crops of a video, contact sheets, screen-insert sweeps, slide captures, page renders) are kept after they were made. They are working files, collapsed under the reply; a picture a video uses (an image scene, a backdrop) is kept. `0` = kept forever.

A legacy Word `.doc`, an Outlook `.msg` or an `.xls` that cannot be parsed has no dedicated extractor and is read as text, which keeps it searchable in knowledge bases (the result may carry some noise; a warning is logged once per process). `true` extracts such files to nothing, so a knowledge base sync also removes the ones it had indexed. Zip archives and unreadable PDFs are never indexed as text.

Hard ceiling, in USD, on the model spend of one run. Requires pricing for the model in the platform's price table (seeded automatically for known models); with no price known, cost is not enforced (a warning is logged) and the other limits still apply. Tokens a model reports only in its total - a provider that returns no input / output split, or reasoning tokens left out of the output count - are charged at the higher of the model's input and output prices, so cost is never under-counted (a provider that returns no split at all logs one warning per run). `0` = unlimited.
Hard ceiling on the tokens one run may consume. `0` = unlimited.

Ceiling on the number of tool calls one run may make: once it is reached, the next model call is refused. Bounds parallel tool use, which the internal iteration limit cannot, but one model response that asks for more calls than are left still runs in full unless `AGENT_LOOP_MAX_TOOL_CALLS_STRICT` is on. `0` = unlimited.

How a tool-call ceiling treats one model response that asks for more calls than the run has left (a parallel batch crossing `AGENT_LOOP_MAX_TOOL_CALLS`, or an agent's or flow's own tool-call limit). `false` runs the whole batch, as before, logs a warning and records the overshoot on the run's trace. `true` runs only the calls that still fit and answers the others "Not executed", so the ceiling is exact. Either way the next model call is refused and the run writes its final answer.
Hard ceiling on the wall-clock duration of one run. Combined with the assignment's own timeout — the tighter of the two applies. `0` = unlimited.
Fraction of the cost and token budgets reserved for the run's closing answer, so an exhausted budget still yields a written result instead of a raw digest of tool output. Clamped to `0`–`0.5`.

When the **cost** budget can no longer pay for the next model call, continue the run on the platform's fallback model (Settings → AI Models → Fallback Model / `DEFAULT_FALLBACK_MODEL`) instead of stopping. One downgrade per run. Only cost qualifies — a cheaper model buys no extra tokens, tool calls, or time. An individual agent or flow may turn this on for itself even when it is off here: it cannot raise the cost ceiling, so it is not a privileged change.

Merge several updates of one calendar event (or edits of one Teams message) asked in the same agent step into one provider call. `false` sends one call per update, as before. The same flag refuses a send (mail, Teams message) whose recipients and body match one the run or the same agent already sent in the last 10 minutes, naming the earlier call; the agent passes `allow_duplicate: true` to send it anyway (audited). After a calendar, mail, chat, work item or presentation write, the agent also reads the object back as the system now shows it, with a list of anomalies of the run (the same object written several times, repeated sends to the same recipients within 2 minutes, a near-identical message, an invitation overlapping another event).

Lets a run still making progress at its `Max iterations` continue in stretches of the same size, up to 1000 rounds. `false` makes `Max iterations` a hard cap again, and a chat message's time limit follows it as before.
Longest single `wait`, in seconds. Clamped to `1`-`3600`. Unset = the value saved in Settings.
Total seconds one run may spend in `wait`. Clamped to `1`-`86400`. Unset = the value saved in Settings.

Identical (tool, arguments) calls in one turn before the model is told to stop and change approach. `0` disables the warning only; the refusal bound below still applies. Set both identical bounds to `0` to disable the identical-call breaker. A warning bound at or past its refusal bound never fires (the call is refused without a nudge) and is reported at startup.
Identical calls before the call is refused outright. `0` = warn only, never refuse.

Near-identical calls — the same file or URL read again with different `max_chars` or options — before the warning. A call that names a paging position (`offset`, `cursor`, `page`, ...; `start` only as a number, a date never) not read before on that target is a page, not a repeat: pages are counted apart and warned at three times this value. A re-call whose earlier answer the platform itself cleared from the context is a fresh ask, never a repeat. `0` disables the warning only; set both similar bounds to `0` to disable the similar-call breaker.
Near-identical calls before the refusal; pages of one target are refused at three times this value. `0` = never refuse.
Fraction of a run's step budget (between `0` and `1`) at which the model is told which tools consumed its steps and asked to finish or report. `0` disables.

How many text windows `read_file_content` serves for one file in one turn, per view (the source, or the `mode="extract_structured"` rendering of an HTML, JSON, JSON Lines or CSV file). Past it the call is answered with an explicit error saying the file's window budget is spent for this turn (the file stays attached) and naming the ways forward (the rendered view, or `code_interpreter`, where conversation files are mounted under `attachments/`), never another window. Images are never counted. `0` = no cap; a negative value is refused at startup.

How many distinct images may reach the model as vision blocks in one turn per 25 steps of its step budget, whatever tool attached them (`read_file_content`, a browser screenshot, a rendered figure, a generated image). The budget follows the steps: an agent whose maximum iterations is 100, or a run its progress extended to 100, may look at four times as many images, so a long visual job (a video, a deck) keeps its sight while it has steps. Enforced by the loop where every tool result is appended: past the cap the result keeps its text and loses its pixels, with an explicit "vision budget exhausted" note naming the files and the notes the agent saved. `0` = no cap; the same file is still shown at most once per turn (a second read returns the saved notes).

How many provider calls one evaluation runs at once: its `llm:` conditions, and the `semantics:` pattern embeddings not kept yet. The same calls are made and give the same verdicts whatever the value; `1` makes them one after another, for a provider that rate-limits parallel calls. Between `1` and `32`; any other value fails startup.

The most distinct `llm:` conditions one evaluation asks. `0` asks every condition. A ceiling bounds the model calls per screened message, at the cost of detection: the conditions past it are not asked (those of `block` rules are kept first), so a rule resting on one cannot fire through that tier. The platform log warns once per rule set with how many conditions go unasked, and the Security Audit reports the control `agents.nova_llm_every_condition` as off. A negative value fails startup.

Master switch for the failure pool. On by default — spending an action on a run the platform failed to deliver is the wrong default, and the pool is what keeps that from becoming free unlimited retries. Set it to `false` to deduct an action for every failure, like a success.
Failures credited back per agent, per user, per pool window. The `N+1`th failure in the same window spends its action normally. `0` closes the pool without touching the switch above.
`json` (structured) or `console` (human-readable). When unset, defaults to `json` in production or `console` when `DEBUG=true`.
The sender name of the emails XTM One sends (invitations, password resets, notifications). Set it to your own, such as "Grand Meridian XTM One".
Connect in plain text, then upgrade with STARTTLS (port 587).
Encrypt from the first byte (implicit TLS, port 465). Wins over `SMTP_STARTTLS` when both are set.

Email the platform's users when a boot (or switching AI on) finds the env-managed model catalog changed: `DEFAULT_MODEL` moved, an `LLM_PROVIDER_

_MODELS` list gained or lost a model, or a capability the environment pins (`DEFAULT_IMAGE_*`, `DEFAULT_VIDEO_*`, `DEFAULT_SPEECH_*`, `DEFAULT_MUSIC_*`, `DEFAULT_DECISION_*`) became available or moved to another model. One email per change names the new default model, the models now available, the ones retired, and each capability with what it does and its model ("Video generation is now available", "New AI capabilities in your platform" when several arrive at once). A capability the environment stops pinning is not announced, and on the first boot of a release that tracks capabilities, those the platform already had are not announced as new. The video and music models are announced only while the Video Studio is on (`ENABLED_FEATURES=VIDEO_STUDIO`), the one feature that uses them; turning it on announces them. While it is off, the speech model is announced for reading answers aloud only, with no word of the Video Studio. Needs SMTP. Whether a change goes out is decided by the boot that records it, from its own configuration, so a pod still running the previous environment during a rolling deploy cannot drop it: a change recorded while this is off (or without SMTP) is sent by a later boot that has both, within 7 days, as long as nobody was emailed about it and it still describes the live catalog. What became of each change (queued, skipped and why, sent to how many) is logged at `WARNING`. A change waits until the env catalog has stayed unchanged for `MODEL_CATALOG_EMAILS_SETTLE_MINUTES`, so the changes of successive deploys reach the users as one email. Emails go out in English from the scheduler, a batch per minute, oldest change first, never twice to the same person: an email whose delivery could not be confirmed (the connection dropped mid-send, a worker stopped) is not retried. Announcements an administrator sends from `Settings > AI Models` do not depend on this switch (see Emailing users about model changes).
`all` (every active user) or `admins`, for the changes a boot finds. Announcements sent from `Settings` go to every active user. The bootstrap `ADMIN_EMAIL` account is never emailed.
Emails sent per scheduler tick (one a minute); the rest follows on the next ticks. Keep it under your mail server's sending limit: a hosted mailbox allowing 200 emails an hour needs 3 or less.

How long, in minutes (0 to 1440), the env-managed model catalog must stay unchanged before the change a boot found is emailed. Every env change deployed before then (a corrected rollout, a second release, a rolling restart with new values) is added to the same email and restarts the wait, and a change reverted meanwhile is never sent. `0` sends from the next scheduler tick. Announcements sent from `Settings` are never held.

How far back, in hours (1 to 168), the model list saves an administrator has not emailed yet are combined into the model changes `Settings > AI Models` offers to email. Every save is kept; a model added then retired within the window (or the reverse) cancels out, and a change the live catalog no longer holds is left out.
Bearer token for metrics endpoint (min 16 chars).

Where traces are stored, `postgres` (the default) or `clickhouse`. With `clickhouse`, traces are written to ClickHouse and still to PostgreSQL, and the Traces screens read them from ClickHouse; any other value is read as `postgres`.
The ClickHouse database that holds the trace tables, which the platform creates there if they do not exist (`default` by default).
Set it to `true` to reach ClickHouse over HTTPS instead of HTTP. Off by default.
The timeout, in seconds, of each request to ClickHouse (5 by default).
Anonymous usage telemetry to Filigran. `false` turns it off: the platform makes no connection to the collector, not even the startup check. Read at startup.
OTLP/HTTP endpoint (`.../v1/metrics`) the metrics are sent to, your own collector for example.
Comma-separated deployment tags (`saas,eu-west`) sent with every metric. Trimmed, lowercased, deduplicated and sorted before they are sent.

Keep every agent tool of an admin - the agent builder, the agent trace inspection and the work-items delegation, in chat and on the XTM One MCP server - to the admin's own, group-shared and company-managed objects, like every other caller: the agents, assignments, runs, traces, evaluations, knowledge bases, skills and other entities a tool looks up, lists or binds. The admin role still counts where a tool checks a permission (a company-managed object, an admin-only setting). By default an admin's agent reaches everything, as the admin does in the UI and through the REST API; the Security Audit reports the default while an agent carries one of these tools, chat is on (the General Assistant offers the agent builder in every conversation) or the XTM One MCP server is enabled. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.
Disable code interpreter at infra level. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.
Disable custom tools at infra level. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Custom tool execution mode: `auto`, `docker`, `subprocess`, `opensandbox`. `opensandbox` delegates to an OpenSandbox-managed container (also used by the code interpreter) and requires the OpenSandbox connection variables below.

Opt out of per-user sandbox usage counting (`quota_usage` rows with `usage_type="sandbox"`, alongside the existing LLM-proxy/agentic usage). Counted by default; set `true` for self-hosted/on-prem deployments that manage their own sandbox infrastructure independently of hosted usage-based billing. Restart required to take effect.

Refuse every Slack event on `/api/v1/integrations/notifications/slack` and every Microsoft Graph change notification the platform cannot authenticate, those of the Teams bot's private and shared channels on `/api/channels/teams/graph-notifications` included. By default a Slack integration with no usable signing secret keeps receiving its events without a verified signature, and a Graph subscription recorded without a clientState keeps working, each with a warning in the log and a Security Audit finding. A delivery that a stored Slack signing secret or a Graph clientState does not prove never reaches what that secret or clientState protects, whatever the setting. The same setting limits what the admin OAuth app's webhook (`/api/hooks/providers/<provider>`) and the LinkedIn notification URL deliver to the admin app's integrations the agent owner may use (for a GitHub App event, those recording its installation or, recording none, whose own token sees it), and drops a LinkedIn notification when no LinkedIn client secret is configured; by default they reach what they reached before, with a warning and a Security Audit finding. That webhook accepts, without a check, a delivery for a provider whose OAuth default holds no webhook secret, and by default one for a provider with no OAuth default (with the setting on, such a provider reaches nothing); both are reported the same way. For the Teams bot's private and shared channels, a notification that does not carry the subscription id and the random secret (`clientState`) XTM One recorded for its channel is still acted on by default whenever earlier releases acted on it, with a warning and a Security Audit finding, and the subscriptions created before 2026-07-02 (whose secret anyone who knows the team id can compute) are kept and renewed; with the setting on, such a notification is refused, the maintenance pass replaces those subscriptions and the ones whose secret can no longer be decrypted (if Microsoft Graph refuses to create a replacement, that channel's follow-ups stop until a later pass creates it), and what a refused notification held back is read back from Microsoft Graph, up to four hours back. Nothing to set on upgrade. See Real-time Slack, Microsoft Graph or LinkedIn events do not arrive and Microsoft Teams. Also in **Settings > Access and security** (**Require verified integration notifications**); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

The targets, comma-separated, a test work item may name for its end notification: an address (`payload.notify.user`), a Teams chat id (`payload.notify.chat_id`) or `team_id/channel_id` (a Teams channel). A test work item is one whose correlation key starts with `retest:` or `test:`, or whose title starts with `Notify retest`. Any other recipient is refused when the item is created or updated, so a platform retest never messages a real person. The sending account's own chat (`chat_id` `48:notes`) is always allowed. Empty: a test item may only notify that own chat.

The repositories (`owner/name`, comma-separated) whose deployments the platform observes. A work item may wait on the deployment of a change (`blocked_on_refs` kind `deployment`) only in one of them, since such a wait is released when a running build carries the merge. A deployment wait on any other repository is refused when the item is saved, with the alternatives: a `workflow_run` wait on that repository's release workflow, or a reason with a start date for the re-check.

How many days a blocked work item waiting on pull requests, issues, deployments or workflow runs may stay quiet before it is shown as stale ("needs a look"). An item whose start date is ahead is never stale on inactivity, and one waiting on a deployment the platform does not observe always is. `0` treats such a wait like any blocked item (the 24 h window).

The tools whose results the connected prompt guard screens, comma-separated: a tool's registered name for a built-in, integration or MCP tool (for example `web_fetch,search_jira_issues`), and `custom:<id>` for a custom tool, with the custom tool's id - it stays screened when its owner renames it. While a company-managed Nova integration is connected, the guard evaluates what a listed tool returns to an agent - the text the agent reads, followed by the text of the files the result attaches (images excluded) - and records each rule match in the audit log (`Security alert`, surface `tool_result`, with the tool, the rules and their action). The result itself is left exactly as it is, and the evaluation runs beside the agent, which does not wait for it. Empty by default: no tool result is screened, and an agent run does what it did before the setting existed. Also in **Settings > Access and security** (**Tools screened by the prompt guard**), where the tools are picked from a list; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

With `PROMPT_GUARD_SCANNED_TOOLS` set, withhold a screened tool result that a `block` rule matches: the agent reads a short refusal naming the tool instead, without the files the result carried, and the result is not reused for an identical call. The agent then waits for the guard's verdict on each screened result before it continues (at most 20 seconds each, the results of one parallel batch evaluated together, four at a time in each platform or worker process); a guard that fails or runs out of time lets the result through. Off, a match is recorded and the result reaches the agent as it is; the security audit reports that log-only mode while a guard is connected. Also in **Settings > Access and security** (**Withhold tool results a guard rule blocks**); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Public chat widget: show only the images the platform serves in an answer (any other image becomes a link the visitor can open, so the visitor's browser never fetches a URL an answer chose), open every link of an answer in a new tab, and render answers without inline styles, presentational markup (`align`, `bgcolor`, `<font>`, ...), SVG or MathML, with links of the `http`, `https`, `mailto` and `tel` schemes only. By default answers render as they always did: an image from any `http(s)` host is shown, an HTML link without a target opens in the page, and inline styles, presentational markup, SVG / MathML drawings and links of any other scheme (`msteams:`, `sms:`, ...) are kept. Script is removed in both modes: script elements, event handlers, `javascript:` / `vbscript:` / `data:` URLs, frames, forms and embedded objects. Links that launch a Windows program with a public exploitation history (`ms-msdt:`, `search-ms:`, `ms-officecmd:`, `ms-appinstaller:`, ...) are removed in both modes too, their text kept, as they are in the Office add-in; app links (`slack:`, `msteams:`, ...) and the Office document links (`ms-word:`, `ms-excel:`, ...) keep working. The security audit (`Settings` → `Security`) reports the default while a widget is enabled. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Public chat widget visitor uploads (see Visitor uploads on the public chat widget): the files a visitor attached are deleted once their conversation has had no message for this many days; a file uploaded and never sent with a message is deleted after a day, and the files of a deleted conversation within the hour. A value below `1` is read as `1`: the retention cannot be switched off.

SVGs a model is shown (a chat upload, a user-message image, a tool result such as an agent reading back the diagram it drew): refuse, instead of rendering, an SVG that declares an XML entity or references anything outside itself - a file path, an `http(s)` URL or another document, in an `<image>`, `<feImage>` or `<use>` or a `url(...)` in an attribute. By default such an SVG renders with that reference dropped - what resvg drew there on its own, as it follows only references inside the document - and an internal entity (an Adobe Illustrator export declares its namespaces this way) is expanded within a bound. Nothing is fetched or read from disk in either mode, and a nested SVG embedded as a `data:` URI (draw.io icons) is checked under the same rules. The security audit (`Settings` → `Security`) reports the default.

While a prompt guard (the Nova integration) is connected, a General Assistant message is evaluated before the model is called and every rule match is written to the audit log (`security_alert`, `source: nova_guard`, `surface: chat_message`, `chat_surface: general_assistant`). By default the message is answered even when a `block` rule matched (the entry records `rule_action: block`, `action: allowed`): the General Assistant was not guarded before, so nothing it answers today is refused on upgrade. Set `true` to refuse such a message with the guard's message, as agent chat always does. The security audit reports which of the two applies while a guard is connected. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

The same for a public chat widget visitor's message (`chat_surface: public_widget`). A visitor has no account, so the entry is written as the guard (`system:nova_guard`) and attached to the admin account the widget acts as (`ADMIN_EMAIL`). With `true`, a refused message reaches no model and its agentic action is given back.

Evaluate the model's answer with the connected prompt guard (the Nova integration): `off`, `log` or `block`. Covered: the final answer of every top-level agent turn (web chat, the REST chat API, channel bots, the chat embedded in OpenCTI / OpenAEV, A2A, the MCP agent endpoints, the LLM proxy, the browser extension, background tasks, flows), the General Assistant's (a transfer's included) and the public widget's. Not covered: a consult's or a transfer's inner answer (its parent's answer is), evaluation runs, the OpenAEV autonomous run's cycles after the first, and assignment runs, whose result reaches their owner and which act on the outside world through write tools. `off` evaluates nothing. `log` returns every answer unchanged and at once, and evaluates it in the background (at most 4 at a time per process and 64 pending, 20 seconds each, the first 20,000 characters); a match is written to the audit log (`security_alert`, `surface: model_output`, `action: allowed`). `block` evaluates an answer before it is delivered and replaces one a `block` rule matches with a withheld notice (`action: block`), where the answer is delivered whole: the REST chat API, channel bots, A2A, the MCP endpoints, the LLM proxy, the browser extension, background tasks, the widget's non-streaming endpoint and a transfer from the General Assistant. A streamed answer (web chat, the streaming chat embedded in OpenCTI / OpenAEV, the widget's stream) has already been shown when it is complete, so in `block` it is evaluated and audited after delivery as in `log`, with `streamed: true`, and never withheld. An evaluation that fails or runs out of time delivers the answer. With no guard connected nothing is evaluated whatever the value. Write-tool arguments (an email body, a ticket comment) are not evaluated. The security audit reports the value while a guard is connected. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

The XTM Hub this platform registers with by default, like OpenCTI's `XTM__XTMHUB_URL` and OpenAEV's `OPENAEV_XTM_HUB_URL`. It is the XTM Hub URL proposed in Settings > Parameters, the one automatic registration uses, the XTM Hub the product switcher and the home dashboard link to, and the address of an XTM Hub integration that names none. An absolute http(s) URL without credentials, query or fragment; anything else refuses to start. A registration token is only sent to it over `https`, or to an XTM Hub on this machine.

The role, in this instance's XTM Hub claim, that means administrator. Matched exactly, including case. **Setting it enables the gate**; empty leaves OIDC behaving exactly as it does without this feature.

**Inbound.** Allow external MCP clients to self-register against this platform (`POST /mcp/oauth/register`, RFC 7591). The endpoint is unauthenticated by specification, so it is protected by a per-IP rate limit and a bounded client table rather than a login. Set `false` to turn registration off entirely (the endpoint then returns 403). A confidential client receives its `client_secret` in the answer, so under `CREDENTIAL_TRANSPORT_STRICT` a registration the platform cannot confirm arrived over HTTPS is refused first (`400 {"error": "invalid_client_metadata", "error_description": "https required"}`). Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.
**Inbound.** Upper bound on dynamically registered clients. At the cap the oldest registrations are evicted; RFC 7591 clients re-register transparently. Values below 1 are clamped to 1.

**Inbound.** Registrations per hour from one client IP at `POST /mcp/oauth/register`. A hosted client (claude.ai, ChatGPT) registers one client per fresh connection, always from its provider's addresses: raise it when many people connect from such a client and it does not use a client metadata document. Values below 1 are clamped to 1.

**Inbound.** Accept OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents (MCP 2025-11-25): a client names its own HTTPS metadata document as its `client_id` instead of registering, which is what claude.ai, Claude Code and VS Code use when the platform advertises it (`client_id_metadata_document_supported`). The platform fetches the document from a public address only (the outbound URL policy, connecting to the address it checked), with no redirect, within 5 seconds and 16 KiB in all, at most 20 fetches per client IP, 10 per host and 60 for the whole platform per minute (refused while Redis is unavailable), and caches it for its `Cache-Control` max-age (5 minutes to 1 hour, 1 hour by default); a known client is served from its cached entry for up to 24 hours more when a refetch cannot be made. Why a document was refused is logged, not shown to the caller. Only public clients with a `client_name` whose redirect URIs are HTTPS or loopback are accepted, and a person still signs in and consents on a page naming the client by its host. The refresh tokens of one authorization stop after 90 days, and sooner once its document is refused. Set `false` to refuse them: such a client then needs dynamic registration or an API key, and its tokens stop refreshing. Also in Settings > Access and security; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

**Outbound.** Let the platform register *itself* with a remote MCP server that advertises a registration endpoint, so remote servers can be connected without pre-provisioned credentials. Set `false` to require every outbound OAuth client to be provisioned by hand — connecting a remote server then needs an explicitly configured client ID. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

Keep a workspace per conversation and run, offer `session=true`, `to_workspace_path` and the `sandbox_*` / `materialize_repository` tools. `false` brings back the stateless code interpreter of earlier releases (no workspace, no tool or argument added).
Size limit of one workspace, in MiB. A call that would go past it saves nothing it wrote under `workspace/` and says so.
A workspace unused for this long is deleted by the hourly sweep. Archiving or deleting a conversation deletes its workspace at once.

An assignment run's workspace is deleted as soon as the run ends (completed, failed, skipped or cancelled). One whose run has not ended is deleted after this long unused, unless the run waits on a person (then `CODE_INTERPRETER_WORKSPACE_IDLE_TTL_HOURS` applies).
Files the `code_interpreter` description and the resume note list; the rest are counted.

Local sandbox only: what each backend process keeps of the workspace contents it downloaded, under the system temporary directory, least recently used first out. `0` disables the cache (every call downloads what it mounts).
A `session=true` kernel unused for this long stops (minimum 30). On OpenSandbox it is also the kernel container's lifetime, renewed by every call.
Local sandbox only: kernels one backend process keeps, the least recently used stopped first.
OpenSandbox only: the longest a check run by `sandbox_run_command` may take; a check's own `timeout` in `.xtm-one/checks.toml` is capped by it. The command's container is discarded after a timeout.

OpenSandbox only: let `sandbox_run_command` run an `argv` the checkout did not declare in `.xtm-one/checks.toml`. Off: only declared checks run, and a refusal lists them. The container has no network and no credential either way.

Packages `code_interpreter(packages=[...])` may install into a workspace, comma-separated distribution names. Empty: installs are off and the argument is not offered. The server installs wheels only, checked against the index's sha256, and runs no install script; a package the sandboxed code imports can import modules the sandbox blocks to the code itself, so list only packages you trust. The security audit reports a non-empty list.
The package index installs read: a PEP 691 or PEP 503 "simple" index, such as a PyPI mirror or proxy.

Host (and optional port) of the OpenSandbox service. The default isn't enforced at startup — a production deployment that forgets to set this won't fail loudly, it will just try to reach `localhost:8090` and fail to connect.
Protocol used to reach OpenSandbox (`http` or `https`).
API key for authenticating to OpenSandbox. `docker-compose.yml` gives the same value to the `opensandbox` service as its own key: unset, that server (v0.2.1 and later) refuses to start.

Per-key container image, as comma-separated `key:image` pairs (split on the first `:` per entry, so a registry:port-qualified image survives intact). Overrides merge on top of the defaults, so overriding one key leaves the other on its default.

Per-key Kubernetes `Pool` binding, as comma-separated `key:pool-name` pairs, e.g. `python:my-python-pool,nodejs:my-js-pool`. A `Pool`'s warm pods run one fixed image, so one name can't back both sandbox kinds — a key missing from the mapping (or the whole variable unset) cold-starts for that key.

The namespace the OpenSandbox server creates its sandboxes and `Pool` pods in. Set, the worker reaps it every minute, and at once after a pooled create timed out: it deletes the `Pool` pods that ended (`Failed`, `Succeeded`, `Evicted`) or stayed not Running and ready past `OPENSANDBOX_POOL_STUCK_SECONDS`, which a `Pool` counts toward its warm buffer and never replaces, and the `BatchSandbox` objects past their `expireTime`. The platform's service account needs `pods` and `batchsandboxes.sandbox.opensandbox.io` get, list and delete in that namespace; without them, or outside a cluster, the reaper logs one line and does nothing. Deleted objects are counted by `xtmone_sandbox_pool_reaped_total{kind, reason}`.
How long a `Pool` pod may stay Pending, Unknown or Running but not ready before the reaper deletes it (minimum 60). Keep it above the server's `sandbox_create_timeout_seconds`.

Comma-separated list of domains/IPs to allow as egress from every OpenSandbox container. Empty means all egress is denied. In a JavaScript custom tool, a `fetch` to a host outside the list is refused at once with the egress-policy message, and a `fetch` to a listed host fails after 10 s when the host does not accept the connection.

CPU requested for each OpenSandbox container (code interpreter + custom tools). Passed through as-is to the OpenSandbox SDK's `resource` argument on the cold-start path. When `OPENSANDBOX_K8S_POOL_NAMES` binds that sandbox kind to a k8s `Pool`, it does not size the container — the `Pool` manifest's own `resources.requests` governs warm-pod sizing instead, so there's no sync requirement between the two - see `dev-docs/opensandbox-pool-management.md`. It also sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` and `MKL_NUM_THREADS` in every OpenSandbox container to this value rounded up to a whole CPU (at least 1), so numerical libraries such as numpy start one thread per allocated CPU, not one per host core.

Memory requested for each OpenSandbox container. Same cold-start-only pass-through as `SANDBOX_CPU`. Both take a bare value for every image key or a per-key list in the `OPENSANDBOX_IMAGES` convention (`128Mi,python-dev:2Gi`: the entry without a key is the default), so the dev images of `sandbox_run_command` (`python-dev`, `nodejs-dev`, built by `backend/sandbox/build-dev-image.sh` with the repository's locked dependencies) can be sized for a test suite without resizing every sandbox. The code interpreter and the custom Python tools read the `python` key, the custom JavaScript tools the `nodejs` key.

Route sandbox traffic through the OpenSandbox server instead of connecting directly to each sandbox's endpoint. Useful for any deployment topology where this process can reach the OpenSandbox server but not the individual sandbox endpoints it hands back — e.g. a process on the host against a containerized server, which advertises endpoints via a hostname like `host.docker.internal` that only resolves from inside containers, or a production/k8s deployment where sandbox pods aren't directly routable from this process but the server's service is.

Container engine API socket mounted into the `opensandbox` service, which starts the sandbox containers through it. Under rootless Podman, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock` (enable `podman.socket`). The service runs with SELinux labeling disabled (`security_opt: label=disable`), which an SELinux host needs for it to use the socket, and which leaves it unconfined by SELinux there; it has no effect on a host without SELinux.

Per-assignment webhook (`POST /api/hooks/assignments/{id}`) only: queue its deliveries that arrive while the assignment is busy. Integration events follow `INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED` instead. Set `false` only to restore the legacy behaviour, where such a delivery was **discarded** and still answered `200`.

Pushed integration events - a Slack event, a Microsoft Graph or LinkedIn notification, a provider or agent webhook - that arrive while every slot of their assignment is taken. `false`: the overlap guard skips them, as it always did (a Slack message is still fetched by the poller). `true`: they are queued, past the queue cap with a warning if need be, and start as slots free. Polled events (email, Teams and Slack messages) are always queued, whatever this says - see below.

One run per inbound event on an agent. A second event-triggered run with the same dedup key (a mail's Message-ID, a calendar event and its modification instant, a provider event id) on the same agent within this many seconds is recorded as a skipped run (`skipped: duplicate of run <id>`, counted in the assignment's filtered events) instead of starting, across the agent's assignments and across delivery paths (a Graph notification and the poll behind it, two mailboxes the mail reached, a delegated pick-up naming the Message-ID). The same window covers an agent account of the same agent on a mailbox the mail reached: whichever of the assignment and the agent account takes the mail first answers it, the other leaves it (the assignment run is recorded as `skipped: duplicate of run the agent account <id>`, the agent account's activity as `already_handled`). An assignment's `trigger_config.dedup_window_seconds` overrides it; `0` turns the dedup off for it. Scheduled runs are not affected.

One answer per conversation from a mailbox an agent sends through, the last line behind the dedup above. Before a Microsoft mail tool sends (`send_microsoft_email`, `send_microsoft_draft`, a reply draft sent, `reply_microsoft_email_in_thread` with `send=true`), it takes a short lock on the conversation for the sending mailbox and looks for a message that mailbox (any agent, any run) already sent in that conversation within this many seconds: its own record of the last send, then the mailbox's Sent Items. Found, the send is refused and the tool answer names the earlier message (when it was sent, its subject, its recipients, its id and link); the agent can pass `force_duplicate=true` when a second message is really wanted. A message from someone else that arrived in the conversation after the earlier send lets the new send go out (it answers that message); an automatic reply (an out-of-office answer, told by its `Auto-Submitted` / `X-Autoreply` / `Precedence: auto_reply` headers or its "Automatic reply:" subject) does not. A new email's conversation is its subject (reply and forward prefixes dropped) and its To / Cc addresses. `0` turns the guard off.

Deliver Microsoft integration-event assignments (new email, Teams messages, replies and chat messages, calendar changes, email flag changes) through Microsoft Graph change notifications posted to `BASE_URL/api/v1/integrations/notifications/microsoft`, within seconds instead of on the 5-minute poll. Only effective when `BASE_URL` is a public `https` URL (not `localhost`, a private address or a `.local` / `.internal` / `.lan` host). The scheduler creates each subscription with a random `clientState`, renews it before it expires and deletes it when the assignment no longer needs it; an assignment whose subscription cannot be created, or lapses, is polled as before, and picks up from the last notified event. `false` deletes the subscriptions on the next pass and polls everything.

Runs of one assignment started from its queue at once (webhook deliveries, polled and pushed integration events), clamped to 1-50. An assignment's `trigger_config.max_concurrent_runs` overrides it. To keep up, the cap must exceed deliveries per second times the seconds a run holds its slot: 30 deliveries a minute of 6-22 s runs keep 8 in flight on average. `1` restores one run at a time.

Queued runs promoted and still waiting for a worker, across the platform. The drain stops there, so a promoted run starts within a reconciler cycle and one busy assignment cannot fill the worker pool ahead of the others. `0` = `MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS`.

Once an assignment's oldest queued delivery has waited this many seconds, the drain alternates its newest and oldest deliveries, so fresh work does not wait behind the whole backlog (nothing is dropped), and logs `Assignment dispatch lag` at `WARNING` at most once a minute. `0` disables both.

How long an assignment's concurrency cap stays halved after one of its runs met an HTTP 429, from a model provider or an integration. Only that assignment backs off; a 429 met anywhere else (a chat, an evaluation, an embedding) throttles nothing. The window starts at the first 429 and is not extended by the ones that follow. The providers' own retries are unchanged. `0` disables the back-off.
Maximum deliveries held per assignment. Bounds the backlog a slow or stuck assignment can accumulate.

Per-assignment webhook only: what happens to one of its deliveries arriving at a full queue (a queued integration event is never dropped). `reject`: HTTP 429 + `Retry-After`, so a sender with retry logic loses nothing. `drop_oldest`: the oldest waiting delivery is finalized as a `skipped` run (visible, payload preserved) and the new one takes its slot. `drop_newest`: the incoming delivery is discarded with a `200` and a warning — no run row is created.

Whether a run paused for human input holds the queue. `true` starts nothing more for its assignment until the approval is answered, whatever the cap - bounded and visible, unlike the old silent drop. `false` lets queued runs start beside a paused run; only safe when a HITL pause leaves no half-written shared state.

Maximum assignments that start queued runs per drain. Only assignments with a free slot are counted: one whose slots are all taken keeps its backlog without taking a turn. The drain runs on every reconciler cycle, on every enqueue and at the end of every run, so the rest follow within a cycle.

Per-assignment delivery throttle, applied before the request body is read. Over-limit deliveries get 429 + `Retry-After`. Raise it for a high-cadence alert feed — the queue still bounds how many accepted deliveries become runs.

Event matching of integration-event and webhook triggers. A trigger created on this version, or whose events are chosen again, matches its event exactly: `pull_request` runs on `pull_request.opened`, never on `pull_request_review.submitted`. A trigger saved on an earlier version keeps its prefix match through every other edit and every copy (duplicate, import, catalog clone); its assignment page says which mode it uses and what it matches, with a one-click switch, and the first delivery it matches only by prefix is logged. `true` applies exact matching to every trigger without editing them; it does not read the old `event_type` key of an agent-builder trigger, which only that trigger's own switch does. Also in **Settings > Access and security** ("Exact event matching for every trigger"); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. See Event matching.
Idempotency window. A delivery whose key was already seen within the window replays the first delivery's response instead of firing a second run.

One turn per chat conversation (a Teams 1:1 or group chat, a Teams channel thread, a Slack DM, channel or thread). The run of a message starts this many seconds late; a later message of the same sender in the same conversation that finds it still waiting joins its turn (one run, one reply, the messages in order and flagged as merged) instead of starting a second run. An assignment's `trigger_config.coalesce_window_seconds` overrides it (0-60); `0` turns the window off.

Consecutive scheduled runs failed on a stale integration reference after which the assignment is paused. Re-enabling the assignment starts a fresh count; a scheduled run that succeeds or fails for another reason resets it; manual, webhook and event-triggered runs neither advance nor reset it. Built-in and per-user fan-out assignments are reported, never paused. `0` disables the pause (runs still fail and are still reported).

On Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat, let an identified user's `@agent-key` (an agent's slug, else its hyphenated name) make that agent answer after the routed one, in the same reply - only an agent whose own channel settings let it answer that message (enabled, set to **Receive** and **Publish** on that channel, past the bot's receive whitelist, private-conversation and only-mention rules). Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action. `false`: a channel message is answered by its routed agent alone, whatever it mentions. The web chat's mentions are not affected by this setting.

The longest text of one message an agent's Teams channel or chat listing shows. A longer message is cut at a word boundary and ends with a `[truncated, ...]` note giving how many characters are left and the exact call that reads it in full (`get_microsoft_channel_message` or `get_microsoft_chat_message`); a message that fits is shown whole. The messages of one listing also share a text budget of 40,000 characters, so on a busy channel the longest messages are cut shorter while the short ones stay whole. A value below `1` fails startup.
