Master switch for the whole Runner subsystem: enrollment, the runner transport (WebSocket + long-poll), and the `computer_use` agent tools. Set `false` to remove it entirely (every runner endpoint then returns 404 and the Profile tab is hidden).

Directory of the embedded runner distribution inside the image, populated by CI at image build time. Only needs changing if you repackage the image and relocate the artifacts. Empty/absent (source builds) reports downloads as unavailable.
Minimum runner binary version accepted at connect (protocol gate). Empty means no floor; a runner below it is told to self-update. Format `MAJOR.YYMMDD.SEQ`.
Cap on active runners a single user (or the company-managed fleet) may have enrolled at once, enforced at enrollment so an unattended roll-out cannot create unbounded records. `0` = unlimited.
Cap on concurrent in-flight commands per runner; a burst past this is refused with a transient "busy" so parallel tool calls cannot swamp one machine. `0` = unlimited.

What a restricted runner does with a file command whose path lies inside its allowed folders but leads outside them through a link (symbolic link, junction, mount point). `false`: it runs, as it always has, with a warning in the command result and the runner log; the security audit (`Settings` → `Security`) reports the default while a restricted runner has allowed folders. `true`: it is refused. The same switch covers a file that is not a regular file - a device (`/dev/urandom`, a serial port, `NUL` on Windows), a named pipe or a socket, as the operating system reports the object the command opened, never guessed from its name - on every runner, full control included: `false` reads and writes it as before, with a warning in the result and the runner log; `true` refuses it. Needs a runner from this release or later; an older runner ignores it. Also in **Settings > Access and security**; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

How long an agent's `computer_use` call waits for a command's result. Unset: as long as the machine may take to report it, counted from the command's delivery - its execution limit (`RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` + 30 s, the wait for its turn on the machine included), then the 50 s it retries a result upload through a platform restart, plus 5 s. That is 205 s with the default limit, and it ends before the command's lease, so a command the wait gives up on is never sent to the machine again. A number: a fixed wait of that many seconds from dispatch. Either way a call never waits past the time the agent run allows one tool call (300 s at most): when that limit comes first, the tool stops 5 s before it and tells the agent the command may still finish, its output then landing in the machine's command history. **Upgrading:** the default used to be a fixed 180 s, which could end before a command near its limit whose upload rode out a restart had reported (see `UPGRADING.md`); set `180` to keep it.

Master switch for relays: relay groups, enrollment, the relay transport (WebSocket + long-poll) and routing an integration, an MCP server or a flow HTTP node through a group. Set `false` to remove them entirely: every relay endpoint returns 404, the `Relays` page is hidden and nothing is routed - a resource already routed through a group then fails its requests rather than calling directly.
Minimum relay version accepted at connect. Empty means no floor; a relay below it is refused and told to update. Format `MAJOR.YYMMDD.SEQ`. The security audit lists the relays older than the floor.
Cap on relays enrolled in one group, enforced at enrollment. `0` = unlimited.
Days the platform keeps the record of each relayed request (destination host, method, status, size, duration - never a body or a header value), shown on a group's `Activity` tab. `0` = forever.

Directory of the embedded relay distribution inside the image, populated by CI at image build time. Empty/absent (source builds) reports downloads as unavailable; relays you built yourself still enroll and carry traffic.
The Kubernetes namespace lab pods are created in. Empty keeps the labs off whatever `ENABLED_FEATURES` says.
The Kubernetes API server. Empty uses `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` / `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT`.
The service-account token, read on every call so a rotated token is used.
The CA the API server's certificate is checked against.
CPU requested per container of a lab pod (no limit is set).
Memory requested per container of a lab pod (no limit is set).
Seconds a lab pod may take to be scheduled and start its workspace container.

Seconds one attempt of the checkout copy into a lab may take, apart from the start budget. A copy that times out or loses its stream is tried once more on the same pod before the start answers an error.
A lab unused this long is deleted by the hourly sweep. `0` = never.
Kubernetes ends a lab pod this old (`activeDeadlineSeconds`). `0` = never.
Filigran's licensing server. At every lab start the platform asks its `/api/ci` route for one short-lived `ci` Enterprise Edition licence per entry of `AGENTIC_LABS_LICENCES`.
The licensing server's API-user token (permission to issue CI licences). Kept on the platform: it never reaches a lab pod, an agent or a log.
`ENV_VAR:product name,...`: each lab container gets the licence of that product in that variable. A licence that cannot be issued never stops the lab; the start answer names it.
Hours each lab licence is valid for (at most 168).

Email of the account whose short-lived personal API key, scoped to the LLM proxy only, is minted for every lab that declares `LAB_MODEL = "live"`. The key is handed to the pod as `LAB_MODEL_API_KEY` and revoked when the lab stops; no provider credential ever reaches a lab.
The LLM proxy as a lab reaches it (`https://<host>/v1`), handed as `LAB_MODEL_BASE_URL`. The host must be in the labs' egress allow-list.
Comma-separated model names a live lab's backend offers, handed as `LAB_MODEL_NAMES`.
Hours a lab's model key is valid for (at most 72); revoked earlier when the lab stops or is reaped.

Origin the headless browser loads the render page from. Empty means automatic: the unified image uses its own loopback address (`http://127.0.0.1:4000`), so no request goes through the ingress and the pod does not need to resolve its own public hostname; a split development setup (Vite dev server + API) falls back to `FRONTEND_URL`.

Render a deck in the same headless browser right after an agent saves it and report what the schema cannot see — a slide body shrunk to fit, text cut by its box, text painted past the slide's edge — back to the agent in the tool result, so it fixes the slide before answering. Set to `false` to skip the check everywhere (tool result, `get_presentation`, `POST .../layout-check`; the viewer then offers no `Layout check` button), for example on a deployment without the headless browser.

Let a browser profile open an application on a private network, on the hosts it declares (operator-network policy: loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses stay refused): its sign-in, the agents browsing with it and Video Studio recordings. Also in Settings > Access and security, where the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. It replaces `VIDEO_STUDIO_PRIVATE_TARGETS`, which is no longer read: a value an administrator saved in Settings > Access and security moves over by itself, a variable must be renamed.

Offer the playable arcade and its leaderboard. Set to `false` to keep only the self-playing waiting animation: every `/api/v1/arcade` route then answers `404`, the chat offers no way to take control, and a `?arcade=play` link (the invitation of the chat embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ) just opens the page. This is the only switch: users cannot hide the game themselves, and it is left out only for a user whose system asks for reduced motion.
Maximum characters returned by one `load_skill` call. Longer content is truncated with an explicit marker naming how much was cut.
Maximum number of distinct skills one run may load. Re-loading an already-loaded skill never counts again. `0` = unlimited.
Maximum bytes returned by one `read_skill_resource` call (files bundled with a packaged skill).

cells: Filigran AI extraction endpoints (override builtin integration defaults).

The address of the TTP extraction service the built-in Filigran AI integration calls. Unset, it is https://ttpextraction.ariane.filigran.io; when set, it wins over the address stored on the integration, and the worker logs the difference at INFO.
Seeds `platform_registrations.approval_policy` the first time a Suite platform (OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenGRC) registers, and only then.
Seeds the platform-wide approval kill switch when the platform settings row is first created — an upgrade, or a fresh install.
Reserved to development: leave it unset.
Bounds for the declarative per-agent prediction extractor.
Reserved to development: leave it unset.
Reserved to development: leave it unset.
Reserved to development: leave it unset.
Reserved to development: leave it unset.
Seconds to wait for TCP connect
Per-orchestrator-run cap: a single agent run may not hold more than this many sub-agent tasks concurrently.
Questions a delegated background task may ask its direct parent (the agent that spawned it, when it is one of the task agent's consult peers) through `consult_agent` in one run.
Self-fan-out: allow an agent to spawn parallel background copies of ITSELF (target `self`) to parallelise a large/independent workload — even when it has no peer handover agents configured.
Max consecutive UNANSWERED `waiting_input` rechecks before a BUILD (plan / author-scenario) run is stopped with a clear "operator did not answer" reason.
The same fast cancel poll for the assignment, sub-agent, flow and evaluation adapters, so an emergency stop aborts their loop between iterations instead of at the lease heartbeat (~20s).
Attempts per client IP per window on the session-less emergency stop, counted before the token is checked.
The window, in seconds, over which `PANIC_EMERGENCY_RATE_LIMIT` counts the attempts of one client IP address on the emergency stop with its token. The default, 600, allows 10 attempts per 10 minutes.
OPTIONAL deterministic per-assignment spread window for schedule-triggered runs (OFF by default).

Automatic retry of runs that failed on a TRANSIENT LLM provider error (rate limit / quota, 5xx overload/outage, connection failure) after the in-call retries and provider failover were already exhausted.

The delay, in seconds, before the first automatic retry of an assignment run that failed on a temporary model provider error (120 by default). It doubles at each further retry, up to `ASSIGNMENT_TRANSIENT_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_SECONDS`, and each wait is drawn at random between half and all of it so failed runs do not retry together.

The longest delay, in seconds, before an automatic retry of an assignment run that failed on a temporary model provider error (900, 15 minutes, by default). A value under `ASSIGNMENT_TRANSIENT_RETRY_BASE_SECONDS` is raised to it.
Upper bound (seconds) for a single blocking dequeue (Redis BLMOVE).
Max concurrent document embedding jobs within one worker process
Retry count for document job failures/timeouts

The delay, in seconds, before a document processing job that failed or timed out is retried (5 by default, fractions accepted). With `WORKER_DOCUMENT_JOB_RETRY_BACKOFF` on, it grows exponentially from one retry to the next.
Enable exponential backoff for document job retries
Emit warning when one document job runs longer than this

asyncpg resolves DNS for every new DB connection on asyncio's default ThreadPoolExecutor, which is ALSO shared by every asyncio.to_thread() / run_in_executor(None, ...) call (S3/MinIO file I/O, the synchronous Bedrock SDK, docx rendering, SMTP, RSS, ...).

CPU-bound document parsing (pypdf, python-docx, openpyxl, xlrd, python-pptx, trafilatura/BeautifulSoup) is offloaded to its OWN small executor (see core/parse_offload.py) so a burst of multi-minute parses can neither block the event loop nor starve the default executor that serves asyncpg DNS resolution.

Logs a WARNING with the blocking stack (sampled from a sidecar thread) whenever the event loop stops being scheduled for longer than the threshold, so a wedged pod produces actionable logs instead of silence before the kubelet kills it.

How long, in seconds, a platform or worker process may stay blocked before the watchdog logs a WARNING with the code that blocks it (2 by default). Values are clamped between 0.5 and 60; `EVENT_LOOP_WATCHDOG_ENABLED=false` turns the watchdog off.

When a document fails to embed for a *retryable* reason (provider misconfigured / down, transient network error, empty vectors), it is automatically re-tried by the autonomous `recover_failed_documents` sweeper with exponential backoff + jitter — no manual reprocess needed.
Base backoff before the first auto-retry; doubles each subsequent attempt (`base * 2^retry_count`), capped at `max_delay`.

30 min cap (was 6 h): transient infra waves (DDL lock storms, provider blips) make a document accumulate retries quickly, and a 6 h cap then parked it in `error` — with the dashboard warning banner up — for hours after the cause had cleared.
Random jitter (0..N seconds) added to each scheduled retry so a large backlog re-embeds in a spread-out fashion instead of a thundering herd.
Max documents re-enqueued per sweep tick (bounds worker / Redis load).

After an admin changes the platform embedding provider/model/dimensions, previously-embedded `ready` documents whose stored embeddings no longer match the new target are automatically re-embedded by the autonomous `recover_stale_documents` sweeper — the same work the dashboard "Re-embed all" button does, but without manual intervention.
Max documents re-embedded per stale-remediation sweep tick (bounds worker / Redis load on a large corpus after a config change).
The reconciler loop runs in the worker process and is the single scheduler/recovery contract for all long-running jobs (assignment dispatch, evaluation runs, sub-agent tasks).
Lease validity; heartbeated at lease/3 while running
Claims before a crashed execution dead-letters
Max executions/outbox events claimed per adapter per tick
Extra slack added to job timeout when computing deadline_at

The age, in seconds, past which the worker's liveness check (`python -m app.healthcheck reconciler`) finds the reconciler heartbeat file stale and fails, so Kubernetes restarts the worker (120 by default). Keep it well above `RECONCILER_INTERVAL_SECONDS`.

Shorter safety-net deadline for *in-process tracing runs* specifically (`assignment_id IS NULL`, no orchestration execution row — created by `agent_chat` for chat-handover / consult / transfer scenarios).

Registers a Jira dynamic webhook for each enabled assignment triggered by a Jira event, so that Jira calls XTM One as soon as an issue changes instead of waiting for the 60-second poll. `true` by default. It takes effect only when the Jira integration is connected with OAuth 2.0, `BASE_URL` is a public `https` address Jira can reach (not `localhost` nor a private IP address), and the trigger filters on a project, issue type, status or assignee; otherwise the assignment keeps the poll. Once its webhook has delivered, the assignment is still polled every 15 minutes, as a safety net. XTM One refreshes each webhook before Jira's 30-day expiry and deletes it with its assignment. Set it to `false` when Jira cannot reach XTM One, or to read Jira by polling only: the webhooks already registered are deleted at their next check, within 6 hours.
Max seconds per KB source sync run.
Maximum time a sync may go WITHOUT reporting progress (a heartbeat) before `reset_stale_syncs` considers it stuck/orphaned and resets it.
Cadence at which a running sync updates `sync_heartbeat_at` so the stale sweeper can tell a live sync apart from an orphaned/hung one.

When a scheduled KB source sync fails or times out, the scheduler schedules an automatic retry with exponential backoff + jitter (`base * 2^(failure_count - 1)`, capped at `max_delay`) instead of waiting the full sync interval (which could be daily/weekly) or hammering a persistently-failing source every 60s tick.

A stuck/stale reset is usually a transient infrastructure event (a worker restart) rather than the source's own fault, so it gets a LOWER retry cap than a genuine error: a reset source retries within minutes and never escalates to the multi-hour backoff a genuinely broken source eventually reaches.
Random jitter (0..N seconds) added to each scheduled retry so many sources that failed together (e.g.

Consecutive-failure count at which the scheduler escalates to an error-level "persistent failure" log line and an admin-facing alert (KB activity event + company SSE broadcast) so operators can act on a source that repeatedly fails to sync.
Consecutive stale-reset count at which the scheduler quarantines (disables) a sync source that repeatedly gets stuck in 'syncing' without a heartbeat.
Consecutive-error count at which the scheduler quarantines (disables) a sync source that keeps returning clean failures — catching permanently misconfigured sources (e.g.

Consecutive permanent-error count at which the scheduler quarantines (disables) a sync source that repeatedly returns permanently- unresolvable errors (HTTP 404/410 - the configured path or resource no longer exists).

The window, in seconds, over which the A2A rate limits are counted (`A2A_TASK_CREATE_RATE_LIMIT`, `A2A_TASK_READ_RATE_LIMIT` and the limit per client IP address before authentication). 60 by default, so the limits are per minute.

Per client IP, BEFORE authentication - covering the anonymous card fetch and the jsonrpc requests that fail auth, which the per-registration limits above (bound to a verified credential) cannot reach.
Two hard ceilings on what one submission may cost, because the rate limits bound the NUMBER of requests and say nothing about the size of each.
A blocking send holds the HTTP response open until the task is terminal, polling the projection at the interval below.
How often, in seconds, a blocking A2A request checks whether its task has finished while it holds the partner's connection open (1 by default).
Task creation deduplicates on the client-minted message id.
How long an external run may hold its lease without a heartbeat before the reaper drives it to a terminal state.

Total life of a task, distinct from the lease above.
Push notifications: how hard the platform tries to reach a partner's callback, and how many callbacks one task will hold.
The number of push notification callbacks a partner may register on one A2A task (5 by default); a further one is refused.

The age past which a delegation MUST re-verify before submitting, and MUST refuse if that re-verification cannot complete.
Ceiling on ONE delegation attempt, further capped by whatever remains of the calling run's own deadline.
How long a delegation may stay outstanding — go without reaching a terminal state — before it is ended and its caller told so.
Largest partner response body ingested before the delegation fails (FR-027).
Consecutive TRANSIENT failures that open the circuit, and how long it stays open before the first retry.
How long, in seconds, delegations to a partner agent stop after `A2A_CLIENT_BREAKER_THRESHOLD` consecutive temporary failures (300 by default). Each further failure doubles it, up to one hour.
How long an attempt waits before handing a live task back, WHEN a callback will report the outcome.
The AGE at which the floor will ask a partner directly about an outstanding delegation — not how often it looks, which is `a2a_client_sweep_interval_seconds`, the loop that runs it.
Whether a partner can reach this deployment to call back.
Where a partner should call back, when that is not `base_url` — a deployment a partner reaches at a different address than a browser does.
Token-endpoint requests per hour, bucketed per client IP.

Pre-signed URL expiry in seconds (1 hour)

How long, in seconds, a request to the S3 endpoint may wait between two pieces of data before it fails (60 by default). It bounds a stalled object store, not the length of a large transfer.

Retention applies uniformly to ALL versioned snapshot types: - `prompt_versions` (per prompt_id) - `prompt_versions` rows that snapshot agent personas (per agent_id, where `prompt_id is NULL`) - `agent_config_versions` (per (agent_id, field_name) — covers temperature / max_iterations / reasoning_effort / etc.) - `skill_versions` (per skill_id) All four pathways call `_enforce_retention` with this value, so a single knob keeps history bounded across the whole versioning surface.
Shared state is a durable cross-run key -> value store agents read/write.
- `resolved` entries are purged by the autonomous sweep once their resolution is older than this many days (kept briefly for audit).

How long, in days, the items an agent moves into an archive entry of shared state are kept before the platform's cleanup sweep deletes them (30 by default). An archive entry stays active, so `SHARED_STATE_RESOLVED_RETENTION_DAYS` never purges it; `0` keeps archived items until an agent drops them.

The size, in characters of its JSON, past which a shared state value is flagged (65536 by default). The write still lands, and the agent that reads the value back gets a warning naming its largest keys. `0` turns the warning off.

The size, in characters of its JSON, past which a write to a shared state value is refused, unless the write makes the value smaller (524288 by default). A write to an archive entry drops its oldest archived items instead. `0` turns the limit off.
Work items are a durable, owned, claimable agent-to-agent task queue.
- An OPEN item untouched for this many DAYS is auto-cancelled by the retention sweep (an audit note is written to `result`), so orphaned follow-ups nobody ever picked up disappear on their own.
- Terminal (done/cancelled) items are purged by the sweep once they are older than this many days (kept briefly for audit).
